headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers -- one on Lyme disease and one on Long COVID -- and does not describe either condition in general; each group here contains a single contributing simulator.
Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper reports any direct medical, non-medical, or lost-income dollar figures, so no cost comparison can be drawn from this evidence.

The Lyme disease paper's evidence centers on diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis with fatigue-related or psychiatric conditions, while the Long COVID paper's evidence centers on objective exercise-test-based work disability and sick-leave status -- these are different kinds of burden evidence rather than a shared pattern.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no direct medical cost, non-medical cost, or lost-income figures; its own evidence gaps state that any dollar-denominated estimate would require linkage to claims or wage data not present in this study.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper also reports no direct medical cost, monetized indirect cost (lost wages, productivity loss, disability payouts), or caregiver/travel cost data anywhere in the document.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Without dollar figures in either paper, a reader cannot compare financial burden directly between the two conditions using only this evidence.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 82% of patients were diagnosed at a late stage (untreated six months or more), 55% had a diagnostic delay of three or more years, and 35% saw 10 or more clinicians before diagnosis.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states plainly that no data on diagnostic delay, time-to-diagnosis, or repeated care-seeking history prior to enrollment are reported in its cohort.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper in this set offers numbers on how long diagnosis took or how many clinicians patients saw before being diagnosed.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 35% of patients self-identified as disabled as their primary work status (women 36% vs men 30%), and 61% reported 8 or more bed days in the prior six months (women 63% vs men 49%).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that an estimated 61 patients (66.3% of the cohort) met an objective CPET-defined work-disability threshold, 75% were on medical sick leave, 13% were currently working, and there was a 62 percentage point gap between the sick-leave rate and the working rate.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers measure work-related burden with different tools -- self-reported disability status and bed days versus objective exercise-testing thresholds and tracked occupational status -- so the percentages describe different things and should not be read as the same kind of measurement.

comparison_rows.dimension: Medical disbelief, misdiagnosis, and diagnostic uncertainty

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 76% of patients were misdiagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition before receiving a Lyme diagnosis (women 78% vs men 63%).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report a misdiagnosis rate; instead it describes a systemic gap in which organ-centered clinical diagnostics 'frequently fail to explain' work disability in this cohort, which is why exercise testing was used instead.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The Lyme disease paper documents being misdiagnosed with other named conditions, while the Long COVID paper documents standard diagnostics failing to find an explanation at all -- these are different kinds of evidence about disbelief or diagnostic difficulty.

comparison_rows.dimension: How each paper's sample may be undercounted or diagnostically restricted

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not carry a claims-undercounting limitation in this dataset; its stated limitation instead concerns a systemic research-design gap in how sex differences are studied.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper notes that every patient in its cohort was selected because they already carried the ICD-10 code U09.9 diagnosis, so its percentages reflect only already-diagnosed, occupational-disease-referral patients and would produce lower or different counts in the setting studied if applied more broadly.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper in this set flags that its sample was built from a diagnostic code, which matters when generalizing its disability rates.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper breaks its diagnostic-delay, misdiagnosis, and functional-impairment figures down by sex, but its authors state the data 'did not include a sufficient sample of people across races or who identify across the gender spectrum' to analyze those subgroups.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports all of its figures (66.3% work disability, 49% ME/CFS prevalence, 79% PEM positivity, 48.9% Bell-Score severity) as single pooled cohort numbers with no breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, despite the cohort being 88% female.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The Lyme disease paper disaggregates by sex but not by race or gender identity, while the Long COVID paper disaggregates by none of these despite a heavily female cohort, so each paper gives a reader a different slice of subgroup detail.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 74% of patients rated their own health status as fair or poor.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that 48.9% of patients scored in the moderate-to-severe disability range on the Bell Disability Scale (score ≤ 30).

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers include a self-reported severity measure, but they use different scales measured in different ways, so the two percentages cannot be read as equivalent levels of burden.

comparison_rows.dimension: What the evidence leaves unmeasured (caregiver time, insurance process)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states that caregiver strain, insurance coverage, claims denials, travel costs, paid help, and caregiving time in hours or dollars are not reported anywhere in the study.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper states that caregiver time, paid-help or travel costs, and insurance claim outcomes (approval/denial, cost of the occupational-disease recognition process) are not reported anywhere in the document.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper in this set measures caregiving time or insurance-process costs, which is a shared blind spot for anyone trying to build a full economic picture from these two documents alone.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper contains any direct dollar-denominated cost figures (medical, non-medical, or lost-income), even though both document substantial functional burden.

evidence.note: The paper's own evidence gaps state no medical, non-medical, or indirect cost data are reported anywhere in the study.
The paper's own evidence gaps state no direct medical cost or monetized indirect-cost data are reported for this cohort.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers caution that their specific sample should not be generalized to the broader patient population for the condition studied.

evidence.note: The MyLymeData sample is self-selected and skews toward higher education and income than the general population, which the authors say limits generalizability.
The cohort was deliberately selected for severity and occupational-disability referral, so the authors say its percentages should not be read as general-population PCC or ME/CFS burden estimates.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers identify a systemic gap in how research or clinical practice currently handles the condition, separate from any single patient's experience.

evidence.note: The paper notes that despite an NIH mandate to study sex as a variable, none of the NIH-funded trials reviewed were designed to analyze sex differences or gender bias.
The paper notes that organ-centered clinical diagnostics frequently fail to explain work disability in this cohort, which is why CPET-based evaluation was used instead.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper documents a sex-based gap in diagnostic delay and in misdiagnosis with fatigue, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric conditions.

evidence.note: Women showed higher rates of late-stage diagnosis (83% vs 76%), diagnostic delay of 3+ years (57% vs 49%), and misdiagnosis with CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric conditions (78% vs 63%) than men.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper finds that the share of women enrolled varies sharply across different Lyme disease study designs.

evidence.note: Mean women's enrollment share was 42% in acute Lyme disease study sources, 58% in restrictive RCT/post-treatment Lyme disease sources, and 77% in less-restrictive persistent-illness cohort sources, per Figure 3.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper measures work disability with an objective exercise-testing threshold tied to a formal occupational-disease recognition process, rather than self-report alone.

evidence.note: 66.3% of the cohort met a CPET-defined threshold (VO2peak < 15 mL/min/kg and/or PPO < 1 W/kg), and all participants had initiated a formal procedure for PCC recognition as an occupational disease through German Social Accident Insurance.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper documents a high overlap with ME/CFS diagnosis and post-exertional malaise within this severity-selected cohort.

evidence.note: 49% of the cohort met ME/CFS criteria, and 79% screened positive for post-exertional malaise, with a 29 percentage point gap in PEM positivity between the ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS subgroups.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper reports dollar-denominated medical, non-medical, or indirect/lost-income costs.
Neither paper reports caregiver time, paid-help, or travel costs.
Neither paper's authors present their sample as representative of the general patient population for the condition studied.
cross_analysis.summary: This analysis compares two papers -- one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper -- and does not describe either condition in general, since each group here consists of a single simulator. The Lyme disease paper documents sex-based differences in diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis with fatigue or psychiatric conditions, and self-reported functional impairment in a self-selected patient registry. The Long COVID paper documents objective, exercise-test-based work disability, sick-leave status, and ME/CFS overlap in a severity-selected occupational-disease cohort in Germany. Neither paper reports any dollar-denominated cost figures, so no cost comparison is possible from this evidence. Where both papers touch related ground -- diagnostic difficulty, work-related burden, demographic disaggregation -- they use different measurement tools and different populations, so the numbers should be read side by side rather than combined or treated as confirming each other.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison rests on a small, non-random sample: one Lyme disease simulator and one Long COVID simulator, with zero simulators in the cross-condition or other groups, as given in real_stats. It is not a controlled study and the documents were not chosen to be comparable to each other; agreement or disagreement between the two papers here reflects only what these two specific documents happened to measure, not a validated finding about either condition in general.

learning_cards.headline: Lyme's sex-based diagnosis gap raises a question for Long COVID
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found late-stage diagnosis rates were 7 percentage points higher among women than men.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any sex-disaggregated diagnostic-delay figures.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers check whether the path to a confirmed diagnosis or occupational-disability assessment differs by sex?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme's misdiagnosis gap by sex is worth asking about elsewhere
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found misdiagnosis with CFS, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric conditions was 15 percentage points higher among women than men.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any sex-disaggregated misdiagnosis figures.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID clinics track whether women and men are given psychiatric or fatigue-related diagnoses at different rates before a Long COVID diagnosis is reached?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID used objective tests to count work disability
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper estimated 61.0 patients met an objective work-disability threshold and found a 62 percentage-point gap between sick-leave and currently-working rates.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report any objective work-disability testing or sick-leave-versus-working figures.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers add objective functional testing alongside self-reported impairment to assess work disability?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID scored disability severity on a standard scale
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found 48.9% of patients reported moderate-to-severe disability on the Bell Scale (≤30).
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report any standardized disability-scale figures comparable to the Bell Scale.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers adopt a standardized functional-disability scale to quantify self-reported severity across patients?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could prompt Long COVID researchers to look for sex-based gaps in diagnosis and misdiagnosis, while the Long COVID paper could prompt Lyme disease researchers to add objective, standardized measures of work disability and functional severity.
